title: Why Is My AC Blowing Warm Air?
h1: Why Is My AC Blowing Warm Air? The Easy Checks First
description: An AC blowing warm air is often a thermostat setting, dirty filter or tripped breaker. Here are the easy checks to try first and when to call a technician.
quick_answer: An AC usually blows warm air because of a thermostat set to fan or heat, a dirty filter, a tripped breaker or switch at the outdoor unit, a dirty outdoor coil, low refrigerant or a failed capacitor. Check the thermostat, filter and breakers first. If the air is still warm, shut it off and have it diagnosed.
body:
Warm air from the vents on a hot afternoon is frustrating, but the cause isn't always serious. Often it turns out to be a setting, a filter or a breaker. Start with the quick checks below, then look at the signs that point to a repair.

What should you check first?

  1. Thermostat mode and setpoint. Make sure it's set to Cool, not Heat, Auto-changeover or Fan. The setpoint should be a few degrees below the current room temperature.
  2. Fan setting. If the fan is set to On instead of Auto, the blower runs nonstop, including between cooling cycles, and you'll feel room-temperature air.
  3. Thermostat batteries. A blank or dim screen can mean dead batteries, and some thermostats stop calling for cooling when the batteries get weak.
  4. Air filter. A clogged filter chokes airflow across the indoor coil. Swap it if it looks gray or dusty.
  5. Breakers and the outdoor disconnect. Check the AC breaker in your panel and the disconnect switch near the outdoor unit. If a breaker has tripped, reset it once. If it trips again, leave it off and call for service.
  6. The outdoor unit. With the system calling for cooling, go outside. The fan on top should be spinning and you should hear the compressor running.

Give the system 15 to 20 minutes after any change before deciding whether it worked.

What if the outdoor unit isn't running?

If the indoor blower is on but the outdoor unit is silent, the house is just recirculating its own air. Common causes include a tripped breaker, a failed capacitor, a worn contactor, a wiring problem or a safety switch that has shut the system off. Some systems have a float switch on the condensate drain that stops cooling when the drain backs up.

If the outdoor unit hums but the fan doesn't spin, or you hear clicking with no startup, shut the system off at the thermostat. Those parts carry high voltage and should only be tested by a technician.

What if the outdoor unit runs but the air is still warm?

Dirty outdoor coil

The outdoor coil releases the heat pulled from your home. When it's packed with dust, leaves or grass clippings, it can't shed heat well and the system loses cooling power. Coastal homes also see salt buildup and corrosion on the coil fins. You can gently hose off loose debris with the power off, but avoid bending the fins or using a pressure washer.

Low refrigerant

Refrigerant doesn't get used up. If it's low, there's a leak. Signs include ice on the larger copper line or indoor coil, hissing near the lines and cooling that fades over weeks. Adding refrigerant without finding the leak only buys time, so we look for the leak and talk through repair options.

Frozen indoor coil

A frozen coil blocks airflow and stops cooling. It's usually caused by a dirty filter, closed registers, a weak blower or low refrigerant. Turn the system to Off with the fan on Auto and let it thaw for a few hours, then replace the filter. If it freezes again, it needs service.

Duct leaks

In many San Diego homes the ducts run through a hot attic. If a duct has come apart or has big leaks, cool air spills into the attic and hot attic air can be drawn in. A room that blows warm while others are fine is a common clue.

Could the system just be undersized or overworked?

On the hottest inland days, even a healthy system may run nearly nonstop in the late afternoon and still sit a degree or two above the setpoint. That's different from warm air. If the air at the registers feels clearly cool but the house is slow to catch up, the problem may be insulation, duct leaks or a system that's too small for the home. If the air itself feels warm, something is wrong with the cooling.

When is it time to call a technician?

Call for service if any of these are true:

  • The breaker trips again after one reset.
  • You see ice on the refrigerant lines or indoor coil.
  • You hear grinding, buzzing, clicking or hissing from the outdoor unit.
  • The outdoor unit isn't running even though the thermostat is calling for cooling.
  • You smell burning or something electrical.
  • The simple checks didn't fix it.

Refrigerant work, capacitor and contactor replacement and electrical diagnosis aren't DIY jobs. Our air conditioning repair team can test the system, find the cause and explain your options before any work starts.

How do you keep it from happening again?

Most warm-air calls trace back to things maintenance catches early. Change your filter on schedule, keep plants and stored items a couple of feet away from the outdoor unit, and book a tune-up before summer. During a tune-up we clean the coils, check refrigerant levels, test electrical parts and clear the condensate drain.
faqs: Why is my AC blowing warm air but the outdoor unit is running?

If the outdoor unit runs but the air is warm, look at a dirty outdoor coil, low refrigerant, a frozen indoor coil or a compressor that is not pumping properly. Replace the filter, then call for service if the air does not cool down within 20 minutes or so.
Can a dirty filter make my AC blow warm air?

Yes. A clogged filter cuts airflow across the indoor coil, which can cause the coil to freeze and stop cooling. Replace the filter and, if the coil is iced over, let it thaw before running cooling again.
Should I keep running my AC if it is blowing warm air?
No. Running a system that is not cooling can make a frozen coil worse or overwork the compressor. Turn cooling off and run the simple checks, then call for service if they do not solve it.
Why is only one room getting warm air?
One warm room often points to a disconnected or leaking duct in the attic, a closed or blocked register, or a long duct run that loses cooling before it reaches the room.
